title: Tazria: the priest must look (Leviticus 13:2–3)
hook: the priest examines in person, never from a distance

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzara'at, the affliction the rabbis read as harmful speech made visible. Your line was words show on the skin. Did you catch a sentence before it left? Today, who decides. Day three hundred ninety-seven.

A rumor reaches you: so-and-so has really changed, and not for the better. You haven't seen them in a year. You've heard it from two people, maybe three. By dinner, you've half decided it's true. Leviticus 13 imagines a camp where a mark appears on someone's skin. Everyone can see it. Neighbors could whisper. Family could guess. But the text gives the call to exactly one person, and it gives that person one instruction before anything else.
screen: `A RUMOR REACHES YOU.` → `EVERYONE CAN SEE THE MARK.` → `ONE INSTRUCTION FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the person is brought to the priest. The text says: when someone has a rising, a scab or a bright spot on the skin, they are brought to Aaron the priest or one of his sons. Not to the neighbors. Not to the group. To someone whose job is to look carefully. Second, the priest looks. The Hebrew verb, ra'ah, to see, comes again and again in this chapter, dozens of times. The priest looks at the spot. Has the hair in it turned white? Does it seem deeper than the skin? Only after looking does he say a word. There's no ruling from across the camp, no verdict by report. Third, the looking has rules. The Mishnah, written down centuries later, says the priest doesn't examine at dawn or at dusk, or indoors, or on a cloudy day, because in poor light a dull spot can look bright. And not at noon, when a bright one can look dull. Even good eyes need good light. Fourth, nobody judges their own. The Mishnah also says a person may examine anyone's affliction except his own, and one opinion adds: or a close relative's. We're bad judges of what's too close to us. Put together, it's a whole ethic of looking. Come close. Look yourself. Wait for the right light. And step aside when you can't see straight. Many teachers carry it far beyond skin: to every time we're tempted to decide about a person from a distance.
screen: `BROUGHT TO THE PRIEST.` · `RA'AH: THE PRIEST MUST SEE.` · `NOT AT DUSK, NOT ON A CLOUDY DAY.` · `NO ONE EXAMINES THEIR OWN.` · then, large: `LOOK, DON'T ASSUME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look carefully before judging. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you've formed an opinion about from a distance: from a story, a post, a single bad moment. Ask yourself three of the priest's questions. Have I actually seen this, or heard it? Am I looking in good light, or when I'm tired and annoyed? Am I too close to judge fairly? Then hold your opinion a little more loosely, until you can look again. The bell holds the time.
Tazria. The portion where the priest must come close and look for himself, in good light, before he says anything at all.
Your line: look, don't assume. Today, before you repeat a judgment about someone, find out one thing for yourself. Day three hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching on judging others draws on Pirkei Avot's advice to judge every person favorably and not to judge another until you stand in their place, and Tazria is often taught alongside it.

fork.setup: you're the priest. it's dusk, the light is fading, and someone is brought to you with a mark on their skin. what do you do?
options: wait for good light to look.
ask the neighbors what they think.
fork.reveal: the Mishnah says not at dawn or dusk, not indoors, not on a cloudy day. even the expert waits for good light.

original.note: Hebrew: "and the priest shall look": the phrase that comes again and again in Leviticus 13.

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient skin inspection.
what it means: come close, see for yourself, and only then speak.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Negaim 2:2 sets the lighting rules; Negaim 2:5 bars examining your own affliction, and Rabbi Meir adds your relatives'.

notes: Mishnah Negaim 2:2 lighting rules (not early morning, evening, indoors, cloudy day; not noon) cited from memory; confirm.
Negaim 2:5: 'all afflictions a person may examine except his own'; Rabbi Meir adds relatives. Confirm attribution.
'Dozens of times' for forms of ra'ah in Lev 13: a count wasn't made; confirm or soften.
Negaim 3:1 (a non-priest expert may examine but only a priest declares) is not mentioned, to keep the day simple.
